item.title: Amazon Cognito SLA Enhanced to 99.99 Percent for Plus Plan Starting November 2026
item.description:
Amazon Cognito SLA Enhanced to 99.99 Percent for Plus Plan Starting November 2026

Amazon Cognito’s Service Level Agreement (SLA) for user pools on the Plus feature plan is increasing from 99.9 percent to 99.99 percent, effective November 1, 2026. This enhancement ensures tighter uptime guarantees for applications that rely on Cognito’s sign-in and access management capabilities.

📌 Why It Matters

Sign-in is the front door to your application. If your customer identity and access management (CIAM) layer is unavailable, users can’t sign in or refresh their sessions, preventing access to the rest of your application. The application’s availability directly depends on the availability of your identity layer.

Many customers use Amazon Cognito for applications with strict availability requirements, such as patient portals and retail checkout flows. They need the services they build on to support high availability. The 99.99 percent SLA provides 10 times better reliability than the previous 99.9 percent commitment.

⚙️ Key Details

The SLA improvement applies specifically to user pools on the Plus feature plan. User pools on Essentials and Lite feature plans will continue with the 99.9 percent Service Commitment.

  • 99.99 Percent SLA (Plus plan): Reduces allowable monthly downtime from ~43 minutes to ~4.3 minutes in a 30-day month.
  • 99.9 Percent SLA (Essentials and Lite plans): Remains unchanged.
  • Existing Plus plan user pools automatically receive the new commitment; no action is required.

The SLA measures availability per AWS Region, calculating the Monthly Uptime Percentage based on 5-minute intervals and excluding HTTP 500 or 503 errors. Intervals with no requests count as 100 percent available.

🚀 Availability Performance

Historical data shows strong performance relative to these commitments.

  • Availability was at or above 99.99 percent in 10 of the 12 months.
  • It was below 99.99 percent in January (99.988 percent) and March (99.979 percent), but stayed above the previous 99.9 percent commitment in both months and reached 99.99 percent the following month.

🛠️ Switching to Plus

Organizations can switch user pools to the Plus feature plan to qualify for the improved SLA.

This can be done via:

  • AWS Management Console: Navigate to User Pools, select your pool, go to Settings > Feature Plans tab, and choose “Switch to Plus.”
  • AWS CLI: Using the Update-user-pool command or UpdateUserPool API operation. Note that unspecified parameters reset to default values.

Before switching, users should compare features and costs in the user pool feature plans and Amazon Cognito pricing documentation.

#AWS #Cognito #SLA #IAM #HighAvailability #UserPools

Source: Planning for 99.99 percent availability with the Amazon Cognito Plus feature plan | Amazon Web Services

item.title: AWS extends Trusted Identity Propagation to IAM Federation and Roles Anywhere
item.description:
AWS extends Trusted Identity Propagation to IAM Federation and Roles Anywhere

AWS has extended Trusted Identity Propagation (TIP) to support IAM federation and AWS IAM Roles Anywhere, enabling customers to grant access and audit activity based on the specific user or workload behind an IAM role.

🔍 Overview

Trusted Identity Propagation (TIP) carries the identity of a user or workload with each AWS request. This allows users to grant permissions to that specific user or workload and trace its actions in AWS CloudTrail. Previously, TIP was available only for users accessing AWS through AWS IAM Identity Center. The new extension makes TIP work for users and workloads that federate directly into IAM roles or use X.509 certificates to obtain AWS credentials, while also simplifying TIP usage with IAM Identity Center.

🧩 How it works

TIP addresses the gap where access control decisions apply to the role rather than the user, and CloudTrail attributes each action to the role session. By attaching identity context from a trusted source to the role session at credential issuance, TIP provides a stable reference for the user or workload behind each request. This context is immutable for the lifetime of the session and can include optional claims, such as a risk score or a CI/CD workflow name.

The identity context propagates through supported downstream requests:

  • Role Assumption: When a TIP session assumes another role, AWS Security Token Service (AWS STS) carries the context into the new role session.
  • Forward Access Sessions (FAS): When an AWS service makes a downstream request on your behalf, FAS credentials carry the identity context.
  • Outbound Federation: With IAM outbound identity federation, the session can request a signed JSON Web Token (JWT) that carries identity context to an external service.

⚙️ Key details

AWS validates the source and attaches identity context through three primary paths:

Path Source of Identity Context Trusted Source Type
IAM Federation SAML assertion or OIDC token External SAML or OIDC Identity Providers (IdP)
IAM Identity Center Username received from identity source IAM Identity Center
IAM Roles Anywhere X.509 certificate X.509 certificates

TIP context propagates to a new role session only under specific boundary conditions:

  • The target role is in the account where the identity provider is configured.
  • The target role is in another account within the same AWS organization.

IAM policies evaluate this identity context to authorize requests, and AWS CloudTrail records it for auditing. For example, Amazon S3 bucket policies and AWS Lambda can utilize this context for access control and audit logging. The identity context is represented through context keys, including the aws:OriginIdentity/* namespace, which serves as the common namespace for identity information across all three paths.

#AWS #IAM #CloudSecurity #IdentityManagement #CloudTrail #DevSecOps

Source: Know the identity behind the role: Authorize and audit with trusted identity propagation | Amazon Web Services

item.title: AWS Introduces GetScopedCredentials API to Safely Scope Down Temporary Security Credentials
item.description:
AWS Introduces GetScopedCredentials API to Safely Scope Down Temporary Security Credentials

AWS has launched GetScopedCredentials, a new AWS Security Token Service (AWS STS) API that enables you to scope down the permissions of existing temporary security credentials. This feature is designed to help secure workloads, such as AI agents, by ensuring they only have the minimum permissions needed to perform their tasks rather than the full permissions of the calling session.

🔍 Overview

GetScopedCredentials provides a programmatic way to generate narrower security credentials from those you already possess. You can assign each agent, sub-agent, or process its own credentials that carry reduced permissions, a shorter session duration, or both, while keeping the original caller’s AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) identity.

Because GetScopedCredentials works by narrowing the credentials you already have, it acts as a building block that you can integrate directly into:

  • Agent frameworks
  • Continuous integration and deployment (CI/CD) pipelines
  • Services that issue credentials to other components
  • Custom applications

🧩 How it works

To call the API, you must have valid temporary security credentials and the necessary permissions to call GetScopedCredentials. You can make the call using the latest version of the AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI) or the AWS SDK for your programming language.

The technical specifications of the API include:

  • Input Credentials: You can call the API with the temporary credentials you already use, including those from aws login, an Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2) instance profile, or an AWS Lambda function.
  • Scope Down Policy: In each call, you pass a scope down policy (an inline policy representing the maximum permissions) of up to 2,048 characters.
  • Intersection of Permissions: The resulting permissions are the intersection of the session’s effective permissions and the scope down policy. This ensures that permissions can only be reduced, never expanded.
  • Session Duration: You can request a shorter session duration, which cannot exceed the remaining duration of the calling session.
  • Chaining Calls: You can call GetScopedCredentials again using the resulting scoped-down credentials to restrict permissions or reduce duration even further. This allows an orchestrating agent to give sub-agents narrower access than its own.

💡 Common Use Cases

GetScopedCredentials can be applied whenever a workload requires narrower access than the session that initiates it. Notable use cases include:

  • Limiting AI Agent Actions: AI agents decide on actions at runtime based on prompts or tool output. By using GetScopedCredentials, you can restrict their actions to only what is required—such as read access to a single Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) bucket—or explicitly strip away risky actions like deleting resources. Run your agents in sandbox environments, such as AWS Strands Box, to ensure they only access these restricted credentials.
  • Scoping Down Based on Runtime Context: Some workloads run under a single IAM role but require different permissions based on authenticated requests. For example, a multi-tenant application with a single IAM role that serves files from different prefixes in one S3 bucket can use a trusted credential broker to call GetScopedCredentials. The broker obtains credentials restricted to only the specific tenant’s prefix and passes them to the worker.
  • Just-in-Time Access: Securing tasks based on runtime data learned only after the workload begins.

#AWS #Security #IAM #AIAgents #CloudSecurity

Source: Scope down permissions of existing sessions using AWS STS GetScopedCredentials | Amazon Web Services

item.title: Amazon Bedrock adds zero‑instrumentation per‑user cost attribution via IAM identity
item.description:
Amazon Bedrock adds zero‑instrumentation per‑user cost attribution via IAM identity

Amazon Bedrock now provides built‑in, zero‑instrumentation cost attribution that traces every inference call back to the IAM principal that made it.

🔍 Overview

  • Bedrock records the IAM identity of every inference caller with no changes required to your API calls.
  • The captured IAM ARN (including session name for federated users) is published to AWS Cost and Usage Report (CUR 2.0) in the line_item_iam_principal column.
  • Identity flows along with organizational tags into CUR 2.0 and AWS Cost Explorer while remaining inside the AWS security boundary.

🧩 How it works

  • Inference requests go through one of two Bedrock endpoints: bedrock-runtime or bedrock-mantle.
  • Attribution operates at the endpoint layer, beneath any tool‑specific logic.
  • When a user invokes a model, Bedrock captures the full IAM ARN and adds it to CUR 2.0.
  • In billing data, usage is aggregated per principal and per usage type for each export interval (hourly or daily).
  • Per‑request cost is not in CUR; for per‑prompt detail you can use model invocation logs or request metadata tagging.
  • Tags appear in CUR 2.0 with the iamPrincipal/ prefix and are filterable dimensions in Cost Explorer.

⚙️ Configuration

  • Enable AWS IAM Identity Center in the management (payer) account.
  • Connect an external identity provider (Okta, Microsoft Entra ID, or Ping Identity) with SCIM provisioning.
  • Configure AWS CLI v2 on developer machines.
  • Enable CUR 2.0 with IAM principal data and deliver it to an S3 bucket.
  • Activate cost allocation tags from the management account.
  • Create an Athena table to query CUR 2.0 data.
  • Configure the external identity provider as the identity source in AWS IAM Identity Center.

📊 Querying spend

  • CUR aggregates usage per principal and per usage type per export interval.
  • For finer granularity, per‑request metadata tagging provides token‑level detail in model invocation logs.
  • With Application Inference Profiles you can tag spend by workload on the bedrock-runtime endpoint.
  • With Projects and Workspaces you can isolate and tag spend on the bedrock-mantle endpoint.
  • In Cost Explorer, filter by iamPrincipal/ tags to see per‑user spend alongside dollars.

📚 Integration with Claude platforms

  • Tools such as Claude Code, Claude Desktop, OpenAI Codex, ChatGPT Work, and OpenCode invoke Bedrock via the two endpoints and inherit the same attribution.
  • Claude Platform on AWS routes inference through Anthropic‑managed infrastructure; usage is visible by workspace and API key in Anthropic’s admin console, and workspace tags flow to AWS billing.
  • Claude for Enterprise also shows per‑user usage in Anthropic’s admin console and its Usage and Cost API, with spend limits enforced natively by Anthropic.

💡 Why it matters

  • Provides per‑user cost visibility without any code changes.
  • Supports four access patterns: IAM users, per‑application roles, federated identities, and LLM gateways proxying to Bedrock.
  • Enables organizations to allocate AI spend accurately across teams, projects, and workloads while staying within the AWS security boundary.

#AWS #AmazonBedrock #CostManagement #IAM

Source: Cost attribution and controls for AI developer and productivity tools on Amazon Bedrock | Amazon Web Services

item.title: Amazon Quick Role Downgrade via CLI Enforces Least Privilege
item.description:
Amazon Quick Role Downgrade via CLI Enforces Least Privilege

Amazon Quick now offers a reliable way to downgrade user roles using the AWS Command Line Interface, filling a gap where the console does not support direct transitions such as Admin to Reader or Author to Reader.

🔍 Overview

Managing access permissions effectively is an important aspect of maintaining a secure and collaborative environment. Amazon Quick supports versatile user management options for various identity types. You can provision users natively or through enterprise identity providers like AWS IAM Identity Center or Active Directory. Regular audits of user roles are recommended to confirm everyone has appropriate permissions.

🧩 How it works

  • Roles are assigned and grouped according to job functions: Admin, Author, and Reader.
  • The principle of least privilege applies strongly to administration; downgrading roles is a key part of enforcing it.
  • For more granular control, consider Custom Permissions, which restrict capabilities within a role tier.
  • Integration with AWS IAM adds permission boundaries beyond the built-in role system.

⚙️ Key details

  • The console does not provide direct downgrade paths for all transitions (e.g., Admin to Reader or Author to Reader).
  • The update-user API also rejects direct downgrades with a “You cannot downgrade a user role” error.
  • Two reliable solutions exist: manual deletion-and-recreation and a CLI method.
  • The CLI step-down method works for legacy BI-only roles: Admin > Author > Restricted Reader > Reader.
  • The same sequence works for Pro users when intermediate steps use legacy roles (e.g., Author Pro > Author > Restricted Reader > Reader Pro).
  • Before downgrading, verify that users are currently Admin or Author. Downgraded users lose ability to edit resources they previously owned.
  • For large organizations, the CLI method can load user email addresses from a CSV file.
  • AWS CloudShell can be used without specifying the AWS Region, as it uses the current console context.

🚀 Availability

Amazon Quick offers two subscription tiers with distinct role sets:

Subscription Roles Features
Amazon Quick Enterprise Admin Pro, Author Pro, Reader Pro Full BI + AI features (agents, topics, Q&A, stories, generative summaries)
Amazon Quick Sight (BI-only) Admin, Author, Reader Traditional BI authoring and consumption

Prerequisites include an active AWS account with administrator access to Amazon Quick, and the AWS CLI installed and configured if using the CLI method.

💡 Why it matters

  • Role-based pricing means Authors and Admins pay a fixed monthly per-user fee, while Readers use session-based pricing—downgrading can reduce costs.
  • Downgrading helps enforce least privilege, a practice recommended in the AWS Well-Architected Framework.
  • Proactively transferring ownership of dashboards and analyses when responsibilities change prevents orphaned resources and maintains business continuity.

#AWS #QuickSight #UserManagement #IAM #Security

Source: Downgrading user roles in Amazon Quick | Amazon Web Services

item.title: Automating Custom Permissions Assignment in Quick
item.description:
Automating Custom Permissions Assignment in Quick

Quick has introduced architectural patterns to automate the assignment of custom permissions, allowing organizations to enforce fine-grained access control across the user lifecycle.

🔍 Overview

Custom permissions enable administrators to toggle specific features on or off for individual users. This allows for precise control, such as enabling financial analysts to author reports without exporting raw data, or allowing external partners to view dashboards without accessing sharing controls.

Permissions follow a three-level hierarchy where settings are applied as follows:

  • User-level: Overrides role-level settings.
  • Role-level: Overrides account-level settings.
  • Account-level: The base level of the hierarchy.

🧩 How it works

Organizations can use four architectural patterns to automate permissions based on their specific needs:

Method Application Scenario
RegisterUser API Applies permissions during user creation via the --custom-permissions-name parameter; common for SaaS companies restricting features like GenBI and paginated reports based on pricing tiers.
UpdateAccountCustomPermission API Sets a fallback profile for any user without an explicit assignment, including those created via Just-In-Time provisioning.
UpdateRoleCustomPermission API Sets a default custom permission profile per Quick role (READER, AUTHOR, ADMIN, and PRO roles).
Event-Driven Automation Uses Amazon EventBridge and AWS Lambda to detect new group memberships (native Quick groups or AWS IAM Identity Center groups) and apply permissions dynamically.

⚙️ Key details

  • Conditional Logic: For requirements beyond native defaults—such as applying different profiles based on group membership—event-driven automation is used. This is necessary because there is no native API for assigning custom permissions directly to a Group.
  • Complementary Strategies: Role and account-level defaults (Scenario 2) and group-based automation (Scenario 3) are complementary rather than alternatives.
  • Provisioning Gaps: Because Just-In-Time federation creates a window between account creation and group assignment, Scenario 3 only triggers upon the group membership event.
  • Enterprise Scale: Account-level defaults allow large enterprises to instantly block new features, such as GenBI or connectors, for all users during security reviews without per-user automation.

#Quick #AWS #AccessControl #Automation #IAM

Source: Automate user-level custom permissions for Amazon Quick | Amazon Web Services
